body: A man in his forties is clearing out his grandmother’s flat on a Sunday afternoon because she has moved into a home and somebody has to do it. In the bottom of a wardrobe, under a box of buttons, there is a school exercise book with a squared paper cover, and it is full of handwriting he half recognises — verse after verse in pencil, no music, no titles, the lines running to the very edge of the page. Some of it is in a hand that is not hers. He sits on the floor with it for longer than he means to, and he could not have told you what he was looking at.

What he was looking at was a printing operation. It is what a congregation does with words it intends to keep when print is not available to it: every line was copied out by somebody in an evening, from a book that had to go back to somebody else.

For a long stretch of the last century, across a good part of Europe, Christians met under governments that took an active interest in what they were doing. Meetings were registered or refused. What was printed was controlled. Congregations understood that some of what happened in the room would be described afterwards to somebody who had not been in it.

It is worth being careful here, and it is worth taking the word surveillance literally. Surveillance is not the same as violence. It is the knowledge that you are being read. It works by making a person do the censoring themselves, in advance, because the safest sentence is the one that could not be quoted against anybody — and the ordinary effect of it, everywhere it has been used, is that people talk less and mean less by what they do say. What is interesting is what happens to the singing, because the singing is the one part of the service that cannot be conducted quietly and cannot be conducted alone.

This band carries 40 international stations in 29 languages, on a dial that runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70. Several of the Central and Eastern European frequencies are on air today — HM 325.40 Polska Inspire, HM 325.80 Česko Inspire, HM 326.80 Magyar Inspire, HM 327.60 Russia Inspire — each hosted in its own language rather than translated into it afterwards.

What a room under pressure does to its own repertoire is a kind of sifting, and it is severe. Nobody sings a line they are indifferent to when the line is going into a file. A congregation that knew an informer was in the room learned to mean every word, because those were the words being reported, and a hymn that nobody was prepared to be reported for quietly stopped being sung. That is an expensive way to edit a songbook. It is also the only editing process nobody can fake, and what came out the other side of it was a body of material that had been through a test the people singing it did not volunteer for.

Compare the conditions under which most church music is now made, which are the exact opposite, and no worse for being so. Nothing sung in a comfortable country costs the singer anything. The worst outcome available in most rooms is mild social awkwardness. That is a mercy and nobody should want it otherwise, but it does have one predictable effect on the words: when a line is free to sing, the language inflates. Total surrender is easy to declare at eleven on a Sunday. It is a different sentence in a room where somebody is writing down who said it, and the second version is the one that stays in the mouth for fifty years.

There is a second, plainer fact underneath all of this, and it is the reason any of that material reached the man on the bedroom floor of that flat. Music survives where print does not. A book has a location. It can be found in a wardrobe, taken away, and that is the end of it. A hymn that forty people know is in forty places at once, and there is nothing to confiscate. Melody is also a preservation format in its own right: the tune fixes the order of the phrases, the metre reports a missing syllable, and the words come back whole rather than as a gist. Paper is fragile in a way that a sung verse is not.
Which raises the obvious question of what you do with a repertoire like that once the pressure comes off.

The usual answer is preservation, and it is a serious answer. Record the last of the people who remember, collect the hymnbooks, mount the exhibition, hold the anniversary concert. That work is genuine and it is urgent, because the generation that can describe the period from the inside is going. But an archive does one thing to a song that it cannot help doing: it turns it into evidence. The song becomes a document about a period, filed under a decade, played to people who arrive already knowing they are supposed to be moved. And a song that is chiefly evidence has stopped being sung.
A hymn in an archive is safe. A hymn in a kitchen at seven in the morning is still working.

A woman of eighty-odd is sitting in an armchair with a blanket over her knees while her daughter tries, gently and for the third time, to establish whether she knows what day it is. She does not. She has the daughter’s name and she has an old address. Then the daughter, mostly to change the subject, starts a line of something she remembers from being small. Her mother comes in on the second word. She sings all of it, four verses, in order, with the pauses in the right places, and she does not open her eyes, and when it is finished she asks again what day it is. There is no book anywhere in the room and there has not been one for years.

Nothing in that flat was preserving anything. That repertoire was never stored in paper in the first place — it was put into people by other people who had good reason to doubt that paper would last, and it is still there when very little else is.

It is only fair to say what this music is actually like. A repertoire shaped under pressure tends to be plain. The tunes are often severe, the harmony is close and unfashionable, and there is more about endurance in it than about victory. It will be in a language you very likely do not speak. And there is a further risk on the other side, which is that a church can end up living on the memory instead of on the faith the memory was about, and that turns into a grievance handed down to grandchildren who were not there.

But the austerity is not a defect in the material. It is the material. Everything ornamental was removed by people who could not afford ornament, and what is left is what a congregation was prepared to be reported for. You do not need the language to hear that. A room that means it sounds different from a room that is performing, in any language on earth, and the difference is audible in the first eight bars to anybody who has ever been in either kind of room.

So putting that repertoire on a frequency is not a heritage exercise and it is not a museum. It is keeping the memory of what the words cost attached to the words themselves, which is the only thing that stops them going ordinary again. The songs were built to be carried by people rather than by paper. Broadcasting them is simply the next set of people, and a considerably easier way to carry them than a pencil and a borrowed book.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

The international part of this dial is arranged on one principle: a station is hosted in its language rather than translated into it. That sounds obvious and it is rare. A translated service treats a language as a delivery mechanism for material that was made somewhere else; a hosted station treats it as the place the material comes from. It means the Polish frequency plays what Polish congregations actually sing, and the Hungarian one what Hungarian congregations sing, including the parts of each repertoire that no English-language station would ever have thought to commission.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 326.20 — Jubilee Praise, in Romanian. Romanian evangelical churches came through the communist decades with a body of song that was carried the hard way, learned by ear in rooms where people had reason to be careful, and much of it is still sung — by people who remember the period and by grandchildren who do not. That is why this is the frequency for the argument this article has been making. You will not follow the words. You will hear a congregation that is not decorating anything, and you will hear it in a house where nobody is watching you listen, which is a privilege worth noticing while it lasts.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone is nearest, press play, and it plays — it is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are really reaching for, which is how the next station gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer. Put HM 326.20 on this evening while you are doing the washing up, and do not sit down in front of it and study it. Let it play in the room the way it was always meant to be heard: while somebody is doing something else, in a house, in a language somebody else’s grandmother copied out in pencil so that it would still be there this evening for you.
